checkpoints.title: Tradeoff duel
checkpoints.prompt: A distributed cache frequently adds and removes nodes. Which placement scheme minimizes remapping?

options.label: hash(key) modulo node count
options.sub: simple direct placement using the current cluster size
options.verdict: Modulo placement is simple and balanced while the node count is fixed, but changing that divisor remaps most keys and can create a cache-miss storm.

options.label: Consistent hash ring
options.sub: assign keys to the next token clockwise
options.verdict: Adding or removing a node changes only the adjacent token ranges. Virtual nodes spread those ranges around the ring so movement and recovery load are shared more evenly.

defend.prompt: Which caveats remain after choosing consistent hashing?

options.label: Virtual nodes improve balance across physical nodes
A hot key can still overload its owner
Replication must still be designed separately
The ring guarantees perfectly equal load

defend.explain: Consistent hashing limits remapping; it does not make unequal traffic disappear or provide copies by itself. Virtual nodes smooth statistical imbalance and let heterogeneous machines own different token counts, while replication and hot-key mitigation remain separate concerns.

checkpoints.title: Ring reasoning ladder
checkpoints.prompt: Reason from the hash-ring assignment and membership changes.

rungs.q: After hashing a key onto the ring, which node owns it?
choices: Every node with a larger ID
rungs.note: The key walks clockwise from its hash position and belongs to the first node token encountered.

rungs.q: With N evenly balanced nodes, roughly what fraction of keys moves when one node is added?
rungs.note: Only the ranges newly claimed from the added node's clockwise successors move, ideally around one node's share.

rungs.q: Why give each physical server many virtual nodes?
choices: To distribute its ranges and failure load
To make all keys replicate automatically
rungs.note: Scattered tokens average out uneven ring gaps and spread a failed server's ranges across multiple surviving neighbors.

checkpoints.explain: The ring's useful property is bounded movement under membership change. Virtual nodes improve how evenly both normal traffic and reassigned ranges are distributed, but do not change the ownership rule.

checkpoints.title: Architecture builder
checkpoints.prompt: Build the key-placement path on a ring with virtual nodes.
checkpoints.explain: Both keys and virtual-node tokens occupy the same hash space. The router hashes the key, finds the first token clockwise, resolves that token to a physical node, and sends the operation there. Membership changes update token ownership without changing a global modulo divisor.

checkpoints.title: Spot the bottleneck
checkpoints.prompt: The ring is statistically balanced, yet one cache node saturates during a live event. Which signal identifies the bottleneck?
checkpoints.explain: Even token ownership cannot split one key: it hashes to one owner. Replicate or salt read-hot keys, add an L1 cache, or redesign the key when writes must also be divided. Adding more virtual nodes only improves range balance.

wrong.Token Ownership: The node owns approximately its fair share of the ring, so token imbalance does not explain the concentrated traffic.
wrong.Other Nodes: Low CPU elsewhere is consistent with a single hot owner but is not the cause of that concentration.
wrong.Membership Changes: No nodes joined or left, so remapping and recovery traffic are not involved.
